brain.intro: Plain-language pictures of how brains handle social cues, feelings, and attention — for caregivers and for Jwan.
brain.ov.care: Different regions work together: the prefrontal cortex plans and regulates; the amygdala flags important signals; the temporal areas help with faces and language. Labels are simplified — real anatomy is more complex.
brain.ov.jwan: Your brain has amazing teams: some parts help you focus and plan, others notice feelings and people. All of them can learn new skills with practice and support.
brain.social.care: The social brain links visual cues (faces, bodies) with understanding (TPJ) and emotional meaning (amygdala). Differences in connectivity can make social scenes feel noisy or fast — supports like priming, scripts, and calm spaces help.
brain.social.jwan: When you read a room, your brain is doing a lot at once. If it feels tricky, that is not a character flaw — it is a signal to slow down, use a strategy, and ask for backup.
brain.feel.care: Emotion regulation is a conversation between threat alarms (amygdala) and planning brakes (prefrontal cortex). Co-regulation and predictable routines strengthen the calm pathway over time.
brain.feel.jwan: Big feelings can feel like a fire alarm. Naming the feeling, breathing slowly, and having a trusted adult nearby helps your planning brain come back online.
brain.attn.care: Attention networks connect frontal areas with deeper structures (e.g. caudate, ACC) to start, sustain, and shift focus. Giftedness plus ASD can mean intense focus on interests and higher effort to switch tasks — accommodations and movement breaks matter.
brain.attn.jwan: Your attention can be super-strong for what you love. When you have to switch tasks, small steps and timers help your brain change gears.
brain.giftBody: Jwan's profile combines high cognitive ability with autistic neurodevelopment. Strengths and support needs can both be true — the goal is fit, not fixing.
brain.gift.vci: Verbal comprehension in the top fraction of children — rich vocabulary and reasoning when the environment is accessible.
brain.gift.fsiq: Overall IQ in the gifted range — with uneven profiles (some peaks and some drains) that are common in 2e learners.
brain.gift.lang: Language skills on structured measures are very strong — social communication can still need explicit teaching and practice.
brain.giftFoot: Numbers are snapshots from assessments; everyday life also needs sensory, emotional, and social supports.
guide.intro: Evidence-informed habits for home, school, and therapy — aligned with PEERS, Zones-style regulation, and structured routines.
guide.golden.1: Presume competence — explain the why, offer choices, and avoid rushing.
guide.golden.2: Co-regulate before you teach: calm body first, then words.
guide.golden.3: Match demands to energy — sensory load, sleep, and hunger change the window for learning.
guide.golden.4: Document strengths and wins alongside challenges — progress is multidimensional.
guide.routine.1: Predictable wake-up with visual schedule or checklist.
guide.routine.2: Short movement or sensory break before demanding tasks.
guide.routine.3: Dedicated time for special interests as fuel, not only as reward.
guide.routine.4: Wind-down routine with low blue light and predictable steps.
guide.crisis.intro: Use a short, repeatable sequence everyone knows. Adapt language to age.
guide.crisis.step1: Reduce input — lower voice, fewer words, more space.
guide.crisis.step2: Offer a safe exit or corner — not punishment, recovery.
guide.crisis.step3: Breathing or heavy work (push wall, weighted blanket) if accepted.
guide.crisis.step4: Return to connection — name the feeling, repair, then problem-solve briefly.
guide.crisis.note: If safety is at risk, follow your local crisis protocol and medical advice.
guide.evidence.peers: PEERS is a structured, evidence-based social skills programme — often delivered in groups with caregiver coaching.
guide.evidence.zones: A framework for naming arousal states and matching strategies — not behaviour labels of character.
guide.evidence.cbt: Thought-feeling-behaviour links can be taught in a developmentally appropriate way with visuals and adult support.
